summary.text: A pyroclastic flow is a fast-moving current of hot gas and volcanic matter that rushes along the ground away from a volcano.
Produced by certain explosive eruptions, these currents travel at extremely high speeds and temperatures and are the deadliest of all volcanic hazards.
Gravity splits the current: dense rock sinks and runs along the ground as the flow, while lighter ash and gas rise as a surge.

facts.label: Speed depends on
facts.value: Density, volcanic output rate and slope

facts.label: Beyond Earth
facts.value: Seen on other bodies such as the moon

items.prompt: An erupting volcano blasts out a mix of hot gas and rock fragments. Why does much of it rush down the slope instead of rising?

options.label: It is denser than the surrounding air
Strong winds push it back to the ground
It cools quickly and turns to liquid
The volcano's magnetism pulls it down

items.explain: Much of the erupted mixture is denser than the atmosphere, so it sinks and moves along the ground as a current.

items.prompt: Of all the dangers a volcano can unleash, which is the deadliest?
items.explain: Fast, extremely hot currents of gas and volcanic matter that race along the ground are the deadliest volcanic hazard.

items.prompt: Two currents of the same density leave a volcano at the same rate, one down a steep slope and one down a gentle one. Which is likely faster?

options.label: The gentle one, since it spreads out
Both move at exactly the same speed

items.explain: A pyroclastic current's speed depends on its density, the output rate and the gradient of the slope.

items.prompt: As a current races downhill, which part stays low and travels along the ground?
items.explain: Heavier rock is pulled more strongly by gravity and sinks to flow along the ground, while lighter ash rises.

items.prompt: A current from an erupting island volcano reaches the shoreline. What can happen next?

options.label: It can carry on across the water
It always stops dead at the coast
It turns back into liquid lava
It freezes at once into glass

items.explain: Pyroclastic density currents can flow over water, with their denser parts sinking into it.

items.prompt: The word 'pyroclastic' joins Greek words for 'fire' and what else?
items.explain: Pyroclast comes from Greek pýr, 'fire', and klastós, 'broken in pieces'.
